MCA President Wee Ka Siong recently said in a media interview that he did not sign a statutory declaration to support PAS President Abdul Hadi Awang as Prime Minister. This is sophistry, his cunning deception.

The SD that Wee signed was to support Muhyiddin Yassin, who was then Chairman of Perikatan Nasional, in establishing a federal government with Bersatu and PAS.

In the 19 November 2022 general election, Pakatan Harapan won 82 parliamentary seats nationwide (71 in Peninsular Malaysia), Perikatan Nasional won 74 seats (71 in the Peninsula), while Barisan Nasional secured 30 seats (23 in the Peninsula). No coalition obtained a simple majority of 112 seats.

At that point of time, Wee Ka Siong’s SD was signed to support the formation of a Perikatan Nasional government with Muhyiddin as Prime Minister.

Wee’s reasons for signing the SD were:

1. He believed the situation at the time was chaotic.
2. He adhered to the idea of “no Anwar, no DAP”, and therefore, supported Perikatan Nasional in forming the government.

If the next general election, be it in 2026 or 2027, once again sees a three-cornered fight between Pakatan Harapan, Barisan Nasional, and Perikatan Nasional, we may again see that no single coalition secures a simple majority. 

We can also be fairly certain that if history repeats, Wee Ka Siong would probably once again support Perikatan Nasional to form the government.

Wee is among the strongest advocates within Barisan Nasional for a three-cornered contest in the next general election. This is because he believes a three-way contest would allow MCA to contest more seats, not just confined to their two incumbent seats.

Since this MCA President has chosen to bring up this issue, and given that he is one of the strongest proponents of a three-cornered fight, he has to make clear to the voters whether he will support the now PAS-dominated Perikatan Nasional in forming the government should the political situation of 2022 recurs.

At least by being honest, voters can know what MCA stands for.
If you trust Wee Ka Siong, pig will climb tree.

"PAS WAS FURIOUS UNTIL THEIR EMERGENCY MEETING. WHAT HAPPENED?"

BY LOKMAN ADAM

The emergency PAS meeting ended exactly the way many expected. All smoke, no fire. After days of dramatic warnings against Bersatu, PAS leaders suddenly went silent after gathering their top leadership behind closed doors. Malaysians were left staring at political theatre without a conclusion.

This is the problem with PAS today. The party wants to sound fierce in public but cautious in reality. They openly accuse Bersatu of betrayal, arrogance and breaking promises, yet when the moment arrives to make a hard decision, PAS retreats into silence.

That is not strength. That is political hesitation.

PAS president Abdul Hadi Awang already laid out serious accusations against Bersatu. He claimed Bersatu blocked coalition expansion, ignored agreements and damaged the spirit of cooperation within Perikatan Nasional. The Perlis Menteri Besar controversy was even cited as proof of Bersatu’s bad faith.

If those accusations are true, why is PAS still dragging its feet?

A political party that truly believes its partner is toxic should not need endless meetings and indefinite reviews. It should act decisively. Instead, PAS now looks trapped inside a relationship it no longer trusts but is too afraid to abandon.

Bersatu, meanwhile, continues behaving like a party obsessed with control and dominance. Since the beginning, Bersatu’s political style has revolved around leverage, pressure and survival tactics. The coalition was never built on mutual respect. It was built on temporary convenience and electoral desperation.

That is why PAS and Bersatu increasingly resemble toxic twins. One weaponises religious and emotional narratives while the other masters political manoeuvring and power games. Their partnership was stitched together by ambition, not sincerity.

Now both sides are exposing each other publicly. PAS complains Bersatu cannot be trusted. Bersatu sees PAS as dependent but unwilling to leave. The coalition no longer projects confidence. It projects suspicion, insecurity and internal decay.

The biggest loser in all this confusion is Perikatan Nasional itself. Elections are approaching fast, yet its own leaders cannot even provide clarity about whether the coalition still has genuine unity. Voters are expected to trust leaders who clearly no longer trust each other.

What happened after the PAS special meeting says everything. Loud accusations before the meeting. Deafening silence after the meeting. PAS wants the political mileage of attacking Bersatu without carrying the courage and consequences of making a final decision. That is not leadership. That is political limbo dressed up as strategy.

Text:
PETALING JAYA: PAS is expected to let Perikatan Nasional (PN) go dormant without formally dissolving it as cooperation with Umno and Bersatu is no longer viewed as a viable option, according to a political scientist.

Wong Chin Huat of Sunway University said PAS now appears ready to shift course and build a new coalition with the Reset movement led by Hamzah Zainudin, as well as Pejuang and Berjasa.

He said cooperation with Umno and Bersatu was impossible as the two parties were large enough to become significant rivals, likening the three-way dynamic to rival suitors.

“The advantage of Pejuang and Berjasa is that they are small and insignificant. As such, they are likely to accept whatever PAS offers in exchange for projecting an image of Malay-Muslim unity,” he told FMT.

Wong added that such a coalition would also free PAS from negotiating seat allocations with Bersatu, while allowing its new allies to contest against Bersatu on their own terms.

He was commenting on remarks by PAS treasurer Iskandar Abdul Samad, who suggested that a coalition comprising PAS, Pejuang, Berjasa and Reset could provide the most stable platform to advance the Malay-Muslim agenda.

However, Iskandar said such cooperation would likely face attempts to undermine it, without elaborating further.

Azmil Tayeb of Universiti Sains Malaysia said that PAS sees itself as capable of operating independently, or alongside other parties or movements, having realised that losing Bersatu would not significantly affect it.

He said this was evident during the last general election (GE15), when Bersatu was shown to be heavily dependent on PAS’s grassroots machinery to remain electorally competitive.

“It would resemble the GE14 model, where PAS worked with smaller parties like Berjasa to form the Gagasan Sejahtera coalition, yet still managed to win 18 parliamentary seats at the time,” he said.

Azmil also said Umno’s preference for contesting solo, overlapping traditional seats, and a complex political history between the parties would make any post-PN cooperation difficult.

“Parti Bersama Malaysia (Bersama), meanwhile, has a different ideology because its struggle is not rooted in Malay-Islam supremacy,” he said.

No More BN, PH or PN: It’s Time for Party Bersama Malaysia 

Rafizi Ramli and Nik Nazmi have officially resigned from PKR, vacated their seats in Pandan and Setiawangsa, and taken leadership of Party Bersama Malaysia. 

This marks a bold and necessary break from the endless cycle of Malaysian politics.

Enough is enough.

For far too long, Malaysian politics has been trapped in a tired rotation between PH (DAP, PKR, AMANAH), BN (UMNO, MCA, MIC), and PN (PAS, BERSATU). 

Every election feels like a repeat: the same faces, the same coalitions, the same disappointments. 

Are you not bored? 
Are you not tired?

PETALING JAYA: Bersatu has dismissed speculation that the party could work with Pakatan Harapan (PH) again, saying it would not follow Umno’s path in cooperating with the ruling coalition.

Bersatu information chief Tun Faisal Ismail Aziz said there had never been any discussions within Bersatu — whether formally or informally — about rejoining PH.

Tun Faisal also said it would not make sense for Bersatu to align itself with PH once again after playing a key role in the collapse of the PH-led government in February 2020.

“Bersatu was among those that brought down the 22-month PH government, blocked Anwar Ibrahim from becoming prime minister, and removed DAP from the government,” said Tun Faisal in a statement.

“(Cooperation with PH) does not make sense.”

He also criticised Umno, claiming the party betrayed Barisan Nasional voters by supporting PH chairman Anwar to form the unity government after the 2022 general election resulted in a hung Parliament.

“At this point, there are no signs that Bersatu wants to become like Umno, which was willing to make Anwar the prime minister through deception and betrayal of BN voters’ mandate,” he said.

Speculation over Bersatu’s ties with PH surfaced following tensions between Bersatu and PAS within Perikatan Nasional. This came after PAS president Abdul Hadi Awang announced that the Islamic party might contest the next general election without its PN ally.

He cited several issues that had strained relations, including the change of Perlis’s menteri besar and Bersatu’s opposition to admitting new Malay-Muslim parties into PN, warning that “patience has its limits”.

DAP secretary-general Loke Siew Fook has since dismissed rumours of Bersatu rejoining PH.

The Racial Arithmetic is Brutal but Real 
Betty Teh | Malaysian Politics 

Malaysian elections are still heavily ethnicised. 

The Malay vote fractures between UMNO, Bersatu, PAS, and now potentially PKR and Bersama. The Chinese and Indian votes function largely as a defensive bloc gravitating toward whichever side appears most viable against conservative dominance. 

In this landscape, any new entrant risks being labelled a spoiler before it fields a single candidate. The cynics are already sharpening their pens. Another party, they say. Another split. Another gift to Perikatan Nasional wrapped in idealism and delivered to PAS on a silver platter. 

This fear is not irrational. 

In a First-Past-The-Post system, a 10% swing in a marginal seat is not a footnote, it is a verdict. 

Critics paint the scenario with uncomfortable precision: Bersama draws educated moderate voters from both communities who previously backed PH, the consolidated Malay Muslim right sails through the middle, and the progressive camp loses seats it could have held by simply staying together. 

The Sheraton Move trauma runs deep. Non Malay voters in particular remember watching coalitions fracture and reform with alarming frequency, each time extracting a democratic price paid by ordinary people while politicians renegotiated their positions behind closed doors. 

The instinct to consolidate to hold your nose and vote for the least bad option is not cowardice. It is hard won wisdom from a decade of watching fragmentation serve the wrong side. 

But here is what the cynics’ argument quietly assumes — that PH, left undisturbed, would have held those seats anyway. That the disillusionment driving voters toward Parti Bersama is Bersama’s creation rather than PH’s inheritance. 

That a party which failed to repeal the Sedition Act, renewed Azam Baki’s contract three times, opened criminal investigations against Bloomberg for reporting what was already in the public domain, and watched its own Youth chief call for investigations into civil society using the language of national security threats — would somehow have retained the progressive vote through sheer incumbency. 

Bersama did not create the fracture. It emerged from it. 

The split happened the moment PH chose accommodation over accountability. 

Rafizi and Nik Nazmi are not the cause of progressive exhaustion. They are its most visible symptom. 

The deeper question is whether Malaysian democracy can afford to remain hostage to racial arithmetic indefinitely. 

Every election cycle the argument is the same — not now, not this time, the stakes are too high, hold the line, we cannot risk it. 

And every cycle the parties that benefit from this logic grow more comfortable taking their voters for granted precisely because those voters have nowhere else to go. 

A captive vote is a devalued vote. The moment you guarantee your support regardless of performance, you have surrendered your leverage entirely. 

What Bersama offers whatever its electoral prospects is the restoration of that leverage. 

It tells PH that progressive voters have a choice. And parties that face genuine competition tend, over time, to govern better than those that do not. 

I joined Parti Bersama Malaysia as an ordinary member. Not because I believe it will win GE16 decisively, nobody credible is claiming that. But because I believe Malaysia needs a politics where ideas compete, where voters are not guilt tripped into perpetual loyalty to imperfect coalitions, and where the argument for change does not always have to wait for a safer moment that never comes. 

The racial arithmetic is brutal but real — and the only way to change it is to stop organising exclusively around it. 

That is what Bersama is attempting. 

Messily, imperfectly, with limited machinery and considerable courage. 

Whether it succeeds or fails, the attempt itself is necessary. A democracy that punishes people for trying to build something new is not protecting reform. It is rationing it.

Reimagining a New Political Future for Malaysia

The recent actions of five Bersatu Assemblymen and three PAS Assemblymen in Perlis, who signed statutory declarations leading to the change of the Menteri Besar — are deeply disappointing. Instead of strengthening the state administration and supporting the leadership entrusted by the people, they chose a path that created instability and political uncertainty.

This episode should serve as a moment of reflection, not only for PAS but also for Bersatu. The apparent willingness of Bersatu’s top leadership to allow such a political manoeuvre suggests that the party itself may no longer be committed to the spirit of cooperation that once underpinned the alliance.

If PAS chooses to remain calm and composed in the face of this episode, it will send a powerful message to the rakyat that PAS is a mature, principled party that does not act out of emotion or personal interest. True political maturity lies in restraint, wisdom and clarity of purpose.

However, calmness alone is not enough.

Malaysia today needs a new political resolve one that is firm, courageous and rooted in integrity. PAS must be seen not only as a patient party, but as a party that dares to confront corruption, cronyism, abuse of power, betrayal of trust and systemic injustice.

The Perlis crisis should therefore be viewed as an opportunity, a defining moment to demonstrate a new political culture based on discipline, integrity, accountability and moral leadership.

Across Malaysia, particularly among the younger generation and thinking citizens, there is growing disillusionment with old-style politics marked by deceit, self-interest and power struggles. Public trust in political institutions continues to erode because too many leaders have failed to honour their responsibilities.

In this context, PAS has the potential to emerge as a unifying force a catalyst for a new political awakening. A movement that transcends party lines and unites principled leaders across backgrounds, ethnicities and ideologies under a shared mission: to restore integrity and dignity to Malaysian politics.

Whether under the banner of Perikatan Nasional, Muafakat Nasional, or any other collective platform, what truly matters is not the name, but the values it represents. The goal must be to build a politics that unites rather than divides, heals rather than harms, and uplifts rather than exploits.

The time has come for Malaysians to rise and demand better leadership leadership that is honest, courageous and genuinely committed to serving the people. It is time to turn away from corruption, betrayal and personal greed.

Only through integrity, unity and moral courage can Malaysia reclaim its future.

Dr. Haim Hilman Abdullah

Two New Parties, Two Different Worlds — Malaysia's Political Landscape Cracks Open
Betty Teh | Malaysian Politics 
18 May 2026

On the same Sunday that Pakatan Harapan held its first convention in four years in Johor Bahru, gathering under the theme "Tekad Madani, Harapan Rakyat" to project unity ahead of GE16; two of its most prominent former ministers were in Petaling Jaya doing something the convention was specifically designed to prevent.

History, as it turns out, did not check the convention schedule.

The Method: How You Build a Party Without Building a Party

At the PJ Performing Arts Centre on Sunday 17 May 2026, Parti Bersama Malaysia founder and president Tan Gin Theam handed the party's registration certificate to Datuk Seri Rafizi Ramli and Nik Nazmi in front of more than 3,000 supporters. No new party was formed. No ROS application was filed. No years of bureaucratic purgatory endured. 

They simply took over what already existed.

Parti Bersama Malaysia also known as the Malaysian United Party, or Parti MU was registered in Penang on 2 December 2016. It was established as a third force intended to serve as a check and balance on both government and opposition. In its entire existence before Sunday, it had contested seats and lost its deposits. It was, in the most technical sense, a registered political party. And in Malaysian politics, that registration is worth more than any election result. 

This is not a new playbook. PKR itself was born from the shell of Parti Rakyat Malaysia in 1999, when Anwar Ibrahim's Reformasi movement needed a registered vehicle fast. PSM fought for ten years to get its own registration. The lesson every serious Malaysian political operator has learned is the same: do not fight the Registrar of Societies. Find someone who already won that fight and buy their house.

Rafizi and Nik Nazmi found a ten year old house in Penang for the price of a handshake and a ceremony.

Why They Did It — The Kamikaze Calculation

Rafizi called the takeover their "second kamikaze mission." "We know there is no guarantee we will succeed. We might lose our deposits in every seat and be laughed at," he said to 2,000 supporters who responded with the kind of noise that suggests they did not find it funny at all. 

"Every day people ask, what has happened? Why are Pakatan and PKR like this? Why are Pakatan betraying their core principles and repeating the same mistakes we elected them to fix? It is hard to answer," said Nik Nazmi. 

The answer they have chosen is not to answer but to leave. 

They vacate their seats. They return their mandates. They ask the rakyat to choose again under a new banner. Whatever one thinks of the politics, the gesture is unambiguous. These are not men hopping toward safety. These are men jumping off a cliff and hoping the parachute opens on the way down.

The five PKR MPs who attended the event: Wong Chen, Bakhtiar Wan Chik, Rodziah Ismail, Zahir Hassan, and Lee Chean Chung are now under PKR membership review. Their silence since Sunday is the loudest sound in Malaysian politics right now. 

The next 72 hours will tell us whether Bersama is a movement or a moment. 

Now Enter the Other Man

While Rafizi builds his new platform on reform and democratic principle, a very different kind of political reconstruction is happening on the other side of the aisle. And the architect is a man who is less nyet nyet nyet compared ti Rafizi.

Datuk Seri Hamzah Zainuddin. MP for Larut since 2008. Former Home Minister. Former BERSATU deputy president. Former Leader of the Opposition. Widely described in political circles as "the Lord of Darkness", an operator who works entirely in the shadows, building networks and pulling levers that others only discover after the fact. 

If Rafizi is a man who announces his moves on a stage to 3,000 people, Hamzah is a man whose next move remains deliberately undefined yet the vehicle he is moving toward may turn out to be more structurally solid than anything Rafizi has just acquired.

The Sacking — And the War Inside BERSATU 

On 13 February 2026, Hamzah was expelled from BERSATU by its disciplinary board alongside 16 other members, all aligned with Hamzah in what had been a bitter internal power struggle against party president Tan Sri Muhyiddin Yassin.

The accusation was straightforward; Hamzah had plotted to challenge Muhyiddin's leadership. The counter accusation, from Hamzah's camp, was that Muhyiddin's allies including BERSATU secretary general Mohamed Azmin Ali had orchestrated the purge to eliminate a rival power bloc that had grown too large to ignore.

What is not disputed is the arithmetic. BERSATU began with 31 MPs. Six left to become pro government independents. 

Eighteen chose to stand with Hamzah. Only six remained with Muhyiddin. The man expelled from the party had more of its parliamentary members behind him than the man who did the expelling. 

Despite being sacked from BERSATU, Hamzah retained his Leader of the Opposition position, the role is determined by parliamentary arithmetic, not party membership. He resigned in April 2026 and was replaced by Ahmad Samsuri Mokhtar of PAS. 

Three False Starts and One Reverse Trojan Horse

Finding a political home was not straightforward. Hamzah outlined three options at a briefing on 14 February 2026: take over Parti Berjasa Malaysia, return to UMNO, or join PAS. 

Parti Keluarga Malaysia, a 90% confirmed deal collapsed when it emerged the party's ROS registration had been rejected in 2022 and remained legally unregistered. UMNO was complicated by its unity government association with DAP, which Hamzah's Malay nationalist base finds politically toxic.

Which brings us to the Reverse Trojan Horse.

Berjasa, formerly known as Barisan Jemaah Islamiah Se-Malaysia, was founded in 1977 as a PAS splinter party. It won 11 seats in the 1978 Kelantan state elections and has been largely dormant since. But it has a national division structure going back nearly 50 years, has already been accepted into Perikatan Nasional as an affiliate member alongside Pejuang, and has strategically rebranded as Parti Berjasa Malaysia, opening its membership to non Muslims. 

The genius of the Berjasa move is its impact on BERSATU. With 19 MPs behind him, a Hamzah led Berjasa instantly becomes the second largest party in PN, dwarfing BERSATU's remaining six. Muhyiddin faces an impossible choice: remain in PN and watch his archrival displace him as the coalition's second force, or leave PN and destroy his own political relevance. 

The announcement is expected before end of May.

The Surprising Openness to Non Malays

Perhaps the most counterintuitive element of Hamzah's repositioning is his apparent willingness to build a multiracial vehicle. For a man whose entire career has been rooted in Malay nationalist politics; UMNO, then BERSATU, then PN — the opening of Berjasa to non Muslim membership is a significant departure from type.

The rationale is partly practical, his expelled allies from Sabah and Sarawak, Ronald Kiandee and Ali Biju, are non Muslim Bumiputera who need a legal home. A Malay only party cannot accommodate them. 

But there is a deeper strategic calculation. A Berjasa that is technically open to all races while remaining culturally and organisationally Malay in its leadership and base gives Hamzah the ability to contest seats across a broader demographic spectrum without triggering the racial branding that limits seat allocation negotiations within PN. It is the same logic Gerakan used for five decades; nominally multiracial, practically ethnically defined. The label serves electoral arithmetic even when the reality tells a different story.

Two Parties, Two Directions, One Fracturing Landscape

Sunday 17 May 2026 will be remembered as the day Malaysian politics cracked visibly along two fault lines simultaneously.

On one side, Rafizi and Nik Nazmi men of the reformist left, building on transparency, democratic sacrifice, and a Penang Chinese party shell heading toward a hung parliament scenario where a clean reform bloc could serve as kingmaker.

On the other, Hamzah the operator of the shadows, a man with 19 MPs, a hundred division chiefs, and PAS's quiet blessing reaching for a 1977 Islamic splinter party and rebranding it as something new enough to contest GE16 but old enough to walk straight into PN without knocking.

Both men are doing the same thing. Recycling the past into the future because Malaysia's political architecture gives them no other choice.

The difference is the direction they are facing.

Rafizi faces the voters. Hamzah faces the coalition.

In 72 hours we will know which strategy the Speaker validates. In GE16 we will know which one Malaysia chooses.

OPINION | Perikatan Does Not Need Another Caretaker — It Needs a Founder

What exactly is PAS’s problem with Tan Sri Muhyiddin Yassin?

Is it the issue involving his son-in-law?

Is it the numerous court cases hanging over his head?

Is it Tun Dr Mahathir’s allegation that Muhyiddin siphoned money from Bersatu?

No.

PAS’s chief problem with Muhyiddin is far simpler, and far more fundamental: under his leadership, Perikatan Nasional is losing.

Not only is Perikatan failing to win new ground, it cannot even hold on to what it already has. Election after election, by-election after by-election, the trend has been unmistakable — Perikatan is bleeding support, slowly but steadily, and the passage of time has only worsened its condition.

What alarms PAS even more is not merely the losing, but Muhyiddin’s response to the losing — or rather, the lack of it.

1) A Leader Without Urgency

Why do I say Muhyiddin does not seem concerned?

Because there is no sense of urgency about him at all.

When an organisation has been on a downward trajectory for nearly three years, one would expect its leader to be visibly agitated — pushing reforms, making drastic changes, reshuffling leadership, rethinking strategy. One would expect frustration, anger, or at the very least, urgency.

Instead, Muhyiddin remains calm. Almost serenely so.

Perikatan has gone from good to bad, and from bad to worse, yet its chairman appears entirely unperturbed. Having Muhyiddin as PN’s leader is like having the captain of a ship who remains composed and dignified even when it is obvious that the vessel is taking on water and sinking.

2) A Temperament Mismatched to the Moment

Why does Muhyiddin project this undisturbed calm?

The charitable explanation is that this is simply his nature. He may have been born with such a temperament, or cultivated it over decades in politics because he believes it projects dignity and statesmanship.

And under different circumstances, that disposition might indeed be admirable.

If Perikatan had already governed for a decade or two, delivered prosperity, stability, and public satisfaction — and Muhyiddin was merely the next custodian of an established legacy — his calm, gentlemanly demeanour might have been ideal.

In such a scenario, Muhyiddin could have played the Lee Hsien Loong role.

Lee Kuan Yew had already built Singapore. The foundations were firm, the structure complete. Lee Hsien Loong was not expected to reinvent the nation, only to preserve and manage what already existed. His calm competence was sufficient because the heavy lifting had already been done.

Similarly, had Muhyiddin succeeded Mahathir in the early 2000s, when UMNO’s legacy was still intact and governance was relatively stable, he might have performed adequately as a legacy carrier.

But that is not today’s reality.

3) Perikatan Does Not Need a Caretaker — It Needs a Founder

Perikatan Nasional does not need a legacy carrier.

It needs a legacy creator.

It needs a leader who can fight from a position of disadvantage, withstand pressure, outmanoeuvre Pakatan Harapan, and claw its way back to Putrajaya. Only after winning can Perikatan begin to think about continuity and refinement.

In short, Perikatan needs a Lee Kuan Yew, not a Lee Hsien Loong.

Just as Singapore would likely have been swallowed by Malaysia or Indonesia had it been led by Lee Hsien Loong at its most vulnerable moment, Perikatan too risks collapse if it continues to face Anwar Ibrahim and PH with a leader whose greatest strength is calm resignation.

4) The Dr Samsuri Speculation — And Why It Misses the Point

This brings us to the recent photograph that has reignited speculation over Perikatan’s future leadership.

Earlier this week, a photo surfaced showing former PN chairman Tan Sri Muhyiddin Yassin meeting Terengganu Menteri Besar Datuk Seri Dr Ahmad Samsuri Mokhtar. The image, shared on Facebook by Bachok MP Mohd Syahir Che Sulaiman — political secretary to PAS president Tan Sri Abdul Hadi Awang — was accompanied by the caption: “Alhamdulillah, insya-Allah.”

According to Mohd Syahir, the meeting took place with Hadi Awang’s blessings and was described as a “casual” encounter following Muhyiddin’s return from overseas. He declined to confirm whether it was linked to speculation that Dr Samsuri might replace Muhyiddin as PN chairman.

Nevertheless, the timing of the photo — just days before PAS is expected to hold discussions on PN’s leadership following Muhyiddin’s resignation — makes its political signalling hard to ignore.

PAS has reportedly proposed two names to replace Muhyiddin: Datuk Seri Tuan Ibrahim Tuan Man and Dr Samsuri, while Bersatu’s Datuk Seri Hamzah Zainudin has also been floated as a potential contender.

5) Replacing Muhyiddin with Dr Sam Is Going in Circles

Yet when I look at that photograph, I feel an unmistakable sense of déjà vu.

Muhyiddin and Dr Samsuri give off the same energy.

If Perikatan replaces Muhyiddin with Dr Samsuri, it risks repeating the very mistake that has paralysed it for years. Dr Samsuri may well offer Perikatan the same calmness, the same gentlemanly restraint, and ultimately, the same strategic inertia.

That is precisely what frustrated both PAS and Bersatu about Muhyiddin in the first place — to the point that they have been trying, quietly and not so quietly, to ease him out for years.

Replacing Muhyiddin with Dr Samsuri may simply condemn Perikatan to another cycle of stagnation, followed by another prolonged and awkward attempt to remove a leader who appears decent and well-meaning, but lacks the ruthlessness and fire needed to win.

Once on top, Perikatan might find it just as difficult to remove Dr Sam as it did Muhyiddin, because like Muhyiddin, Dr Sam also has a nice guy vibe. Nobody likes to be the one to remove a nice guy, because it makes you look like a nasty guy, even if the nice guy deserves to be removed, because he is a weak guy. This problem of removing a nice guy, might be why it has taken Perikatan so long to remove Muhyiddin, despite the fact that he has provided ineffective leadership for years. 

6) Insanity, the Titanic, and the Violin

Einstein famously defined insanity as doing the same thing repeatedly while expecting a different result.

Replacing Muhyiddin with Dr Samsuri fits that definition perfectly.

Perhaps, after Perikatan has won power, stabilised governance, and secured broad public approval, someone like Dr Samsuri could serve as a capable legacy carrier.

But to put him in charge now — when Perikatan must charge uphill, under siege, against a well-entrenched Pakatan Harapan — is like appointing the bandleader of the Titanic as captain. 

All that is going to happen is that the Dr Sam, like Muhyiddin, will be playing the violin calmly, as the titanic called Perikatan continues to sink to the bottom of the ocean.

Beliau menjelaskan bahawa peruntukan Perlembagaan PN membezakan dengan jelas antara keanggotaan Majlis Presiden dan jawatan Pengerusi Perikatan Nasional, di mana Majlis Presiden secara khusus diwajibkan dianggotai oleh semua Presiden parti anggota, namun syarat yang sama tidak terpakai kepada jawatan Pengerusi.

“Majlis Presiden hendaklah dianggotai oleh Presiden parti-parti anggota. Itu jelas dalam Perlembagaan. Tetapi bagi jawatan Pengerusi Perikatan Nasional, tiada satu pun peruntukan yang menyatakan bahawa ia mesti dipilih daripada kalangan Presiden parti,” katanya dalam sidang media, di sini semalam.

Menurut Takiyuddin, Pengerusi Perikatan Nasional adalah Pengerusi Majlis Tertinggi dan hendaklah dipilih oleh ahli-ahli Majlis Tertinggi serta memegang jawatan tersebut selagi dikehendaki oleh majlis berkenaan, tanpa sebarang syarat tambahan berkaitan jawatan dalam parti komponen.

Beliau menegaskan, dari sudut penggubalan undang-undang, sekiranya Perlembagaan bermaksud mengehadkan jawatan Pengerusi kepada Presiden parti anggota, perkara itu pasti dinyatakan secara jelas sebagaimana peruntukan keanggotaan Majlis Presiden, namun peruntukan sedemikian tidak wujud.

“Dari segi drafting undang-undang, kalau itu maksudnya, maksudnya untuk pengurusi PN ini mesti presiden, dia mesti ken letak (dalam perlembagaan). Ujarnya.

Sehubungan itu, katanya, PAS berpandangan bahawa sekiranya parti-parti anggota bersetuju PAS menjadi parti yang mengetuai Perikatan Nasional, maka mana-mana individu yang dicalonkan oleh PAS dan dipersetujui Majlis Tertinggi adalah layak untuk dipilih sebagai Pengerusi, dan tidak semestinya Presiden PAS.

“So, whoever nominated or proposed by PAS to be elected as chairman of Perikatan Nasional, he is qualified. Not necessarily president of PAS and based on the provision in the constitution. Katanya.

Takiyuddin turut merujuk amalan sebelum ini apabila Perikatan Nasional bersetuju melantik Bersatu sebagai parti yang mengetuai gabungan, dan calon Pengerusi yang dicalonkan oleh Bersatu diterima oleh parti-parti anggota, sambil menegaskan bahawa hakikat Pengerusi sebelum ini merupakan Presiden parti anggota tidak mewujudkan keperluan bahawa Pengerusi baharu juga mesti datang daripada kalangan Presiden parti.

All elections before 2018 were always about electing a stronger opposition. Barisan Nasional was always the only government we knew. Pakatan Harapan and all other previous opposition coalitions were supposedly the permanent opposition. 

Now, things have changed. This GE15 is a competition of three potential governments - Pakatan Harapan, Barisan Nasional, and Perikatan Nasional. 

Pakatan Harapan has a clear choice of Prime Minister in Dato’ Seri Anwar Ibrahim.

BN has named Datuk Seri Ismail Sabri Yaakob but most likely would see UMNO President Datuk Seri Ahmad Zahid Hamidi as Prime Minister should it win a majority. PN offers Tan Sri Muhyiddin Yassin who has been tainted as leader of a “kerajaan gagal” (failed government) during Covid-19 pandemic. 

Pakatan Harapan also has a talent pool of multiracial and nationally known leaders who are sincere, competent and visionary. Both BN and PN have less competent leaders.  

All opinion polls published in the past few days placed Pakatan Harapan at the top with between 80 and 95 parliamentary seats nationally, and with a significant number of other seats in the “too-close-to-call” category, which will likely add to Pakatan Harapan’s column in the event that voter turnout exceeds 80%. 

I am putting Pakatan Harapan’s seat count at 100 and above out of the total 222 seats. If turnout is very high across the nation, Pakatan Harapan may have a chance to reach 112 or very close to the number on its own. 

PN, in particular PAS, is likely to make gains in Perlis and the seats east of the Banjaran Titiwangsa, at the expense of BN.  

There is now a distinct possibility that BN might end up at number 3 in terms of seat count in the Peninsula, after Pakatan Harapan and PN.  

It is not difficult to explain this logic: if BN  suffers a massive bleeding of its base vote, even if those votes go to PN in the Peninsula’s west coast, such a shift would benefit Pakatan Harapan, which will further deplete the number of seats BN would win. Whereas in Perlis and the east coast, BN  may suffer more losses due to the sheer hatred among Malay voters against Zahid Hamidi.

The greatest irony of the UMNO-led “Malay unity” coalition is that all the parties - UMNO, Bersatu and PAS were always suspicious of each other. UMNO had tried to eat up Bersatu for the past two years, successfully  kicking out Prime Minister Muhyiddin out of office. PAS keeps on changing partners, yesterday with UMNO, today with Bersatu, tomorrow, who knows.  

I believe PAS will likely ditch Bersatu after GE15 if PN fails to win power or form a coalition government with other parties. 

An important lesson for all: a sustainable governing coalition in Malaysia has to be one that is accepted and embraced by all ethnic groups and able to win some seats or have partners in Sabah and Sarawak. This is the Pakatan Harapan formula. It represents the broadest Malaysian spectrum possible. 

All other forces such as BN and PN that try to divide Malaysia would never win enough votes from middle ground Malaysians who are increasingly more mature and less susceptible to racial and religious incitements. 

I hope Pakatan Harapan will win an outright 111 seats tomorrow, and be given the chance to govern well for the next five years to prove that Malaysia can prosper without too much racial and religious prejudices.   

A Pakatan Harapan government that cares will help many families live a much better economic life and help steer the nation forward during turbulent times in the global economy. We need a dynamic yet humane economy for all.  

A Pakatan Harapan government will sustain a democracy with institutions that have integrity. Enough of corruption and cronyism. 

A Pakatan Harapan government will see Malaysians believing in the idea that Malaysia can be a nation that is filled with hope, potentials and possibilities. 

The votes you cast tomorrow will change the nation for the better, and we shall remember the day as the beginning of a new era which hopefully will last for years if not decades. 

Let's give this nation a chance for rebuilding under the leadership of Dato' Seri Anwar Ibrahim.

Let's give Malaysia a chance.

Kapendam II Sriwijaya Kolonel Eko Syah Putra Siregar mengungkapkan, ada setoran atau bagi-bagi uang antara personel aparat keamanan maupun anggota militer dari gelaran perjudian sabung ayam di Negara Batin, Way Kanan, Lampung. Ini diduga sebagai akar penembakan tiga anggota kepolisian oleh dua prajurit TNI yang terjadi di Kampung Karang Manik, Senin 17 Maret 2025 lalu.

Kapendam menyampaikan, setoran dan bagi-bagi uang tersebut merupakan komitmen antara kepolisian dan militer di Negara Batin. Komitmen itu berupa ‘pengamanan’ bisnis perjudian sabung ayam di Kampung Karang Manik tersebut. Keterangan itu diperoleh dari hasil pemeriksaan internal terhadap Kopka Basarsyah dan Peltu Lubis, pemilik lokasi perjudian sabung ayam. Kedua aggota TNI yang sudah mengakui dan menyerahkan diri sebagai pelaku penembakan yang menewaskan tiga personel Polri.

Sementara itu, Kepolisian Daerah (Polda) Lampung meminta pihak yang menyebarkan isu ada setoran diterima anggota dari aktivitas judi sabung ayam di Kabupaten Way Kanan menunjukkan bukti. Bila benar terbukti, maka anggota yang bersalah akan diproses. 

‘’Jadi isunya kan disebutkan baik Koramil, maupun Polsek di sana menerima setoran, kalau memang iya langsung ditindaklanjuti dan saya yakin dari TNI juga akan melakukan penindakan kalau memang benar,’’ kata Kapolda Lampung Irjen Pol Helmy Santika dalam keterangannya, di Provinsi Lampung, Sabtu.

Menurutnya, isu yang beredar bahwa tragedi penembakan dipicu masalah setoran adalah asumsi tak mendasar. Ia mengatakan, kalaupun memang ada setoran, itu tetap tidak menghilangkan fakta penembakan yang menyebabkan tiga orang meninggal dunia.

Perpecahan antara Parti Islam Se-Malaysia (PAS) dan Parti Pribumi Bersatu Malaysia (BERSATU) dalam gabungan Perikatan Nasional (PN) kelihatan "semakin ketara". Hal ini  dinyatakan oleh felo Geostrategis dan Felo Kanan Akademi Penyelidikan Strategik Nusantara (NASR), Profesor Dr. Azmi Hassan, selepas Naib Presiden PAS, Datuk Mohd Amar Abdullah, mengaburkan gambar sepanduk PN yang digantung di lokasi ceramah baru-baru ini.

Memetik laporan Free Malaysia Today (FMT), Azmi Hassan berkata, hubungan tegang antara dua komponen PN ini mula kelihatan semasa kempen pilihan raya kecil Kuala Kubu Baharu dua bulan lalu. 

"Apa yang cuba ditunjukkan oleh PAS ialah mereka boleh bergerak sendirian tanpa Bersatu. Ini benar terutamanya di kawasan seperti Sungai Bakap dan lain-lain di mana pengundi Melayu membentuk lebih 60% hingga 70% daripada jumlah pengundi," katanya kepada FMT. 

Azmi menambah, gambar yang dimuat naik oleh Amar juga menguatkan spekulasi bahawa PAS mungkin terlibat dalam "perbincangan" untuk bekerjasama dengan kerajaan perpaduan pimpinan Perdana Menteri Anwar Ibrahim. 

Minggu lalu, jurucakap kerajaan perpaduan Fahmi Fadzil enggan mengulas mengenai spekulasi PAS menyertai gabungan perpaduan, manakala beberapa pemimpin PAS menafikan dakwaan tersebut. Walau bagaimanapun, Azmi berpendapat perbincangan tersebut mungkin lebih kepada usaha menjalinkan hubungan dengan Putrajaya. 

"Saya rasa PAS cuba untuk lebih mesra dengan kerajaan persekutuan, bukan khusus dengan Pakatan Harapan atau UMNO," katanya lagi. 

Amar, yang juga Speaker Dewan Undangan Negeri Kelantan, pada 24 Jun lalu memuat naik beberapa gambar dirinya berucap dalam ceramah semasa kempen pilihan raya kecil Sungai Bakap. Enam daripada gambar tersebut kelihatan mengaburkan sepanduk PN. 

Namun, Pensyarah Kanan di Pusat Pengajian Sains Kemasyarakatan, Universiti Sains Malaysia (USM) Dr Azmil Mohd Tayeb menegaskan untuk tidak membuat kesimpulan terburu-buru mengenai perkara ini. 

"Saya tidak akan terlalu menekankan perkara ini. Kemungkinan PAS menyertai kerajaan Madani adalah tipis selagi DAP berada dalam kerajaan," katanya.

“Rakan-rakan dalam UMNO, marilah bersama kami. Kita nak kuatkan orang Melayu, pegang kuasa bersungguh-sungguh. Negara ini siasah politiknya mesti dipegang dan dikawal oleh orang Islam Melayu.

“Bila Melayu dan Islam kuat, bangsa lain juga akan hidup selamat, bebas dan harmoni di negara ini,” katanya ketika berucap pada majlis Pelancaran Jentera Pilihan Raya PAS Kawasan Padang Terap, pada Rabu.

Menurut beliau, PAS tidak pernah melupakan detik kerjasama bersama UMNO menerusi Muafakat Nasional (MN) yang disifatkan berjaya menyatukan orang Melayu dan Islam sehingga mewujudkan semangat baharu kalangan rakyat di peringkat akar umbi.

“Kita dengan UMNO pernah berkawan bawah Muafakat Nasional, kita tak pernah lupa saat manis di peringkat akar umbi.

Bagaimanapun, Sanusi tegaskan, PAS dan UMNO bukan lagi rakan politik pada masa kini selepas UMNO mengambil keputusan bekerjasama dengan DAP dan PKR bagi membentuk Kerajaan Perpaduan.

Menurutnya, tindakan itu berlaku selepas Presiden UMNO, Datuk Seri Dr Ahmad Zahid Hamidi menarik parti tersebut keluar daripada Muafakat Nasional.

“Kerana kepentingan peribadi untuk selamatkan diri daripada kes mahkamah, UMNO dibawa berpakat dengan DAP dan PKR. Mereka mula cari habuan, ramai pemimpin yang kalah dalam pilihan raya dilantik memegang jawatan lembaga pengarah di sana sini tanpa mengambil kira kelayakan atau pengalaman,” ujarnya.

Pengerusi PN Kedah itu berkata, UMNO pernah meminda perlembagaan parti itu dengan memasukkan perjuangan Islam, selepas menjalinkan kerjasama dengan PAS menerusi Muafakat Nasional.

Namun katanya, parti itu kini lebih memberi tumpuan kepada usaha mendapatkan semula kuasa politik termasuk menyerang pentadbiran Kerajaan Negeri Kedah.

“Mereka nak ambil alih kuasa di sini. Kalau nak lawan kita, buatlah kerja elok-elok, tetapi hakikatnya kita buat lebih baik daripada ketika mereka memerintah dahulu,” katanya.

Ketua Penerangan PAS, Ahmad Fadhli Shaari berkata tuduhan kononnya PAS gagal memberi maklum balas sepanjang krisis dalam Perikatan Nasional (PN) adalah fitnah yang tidak berasas.

“PAS masih menyimpan rekod komunikasi terperinci antara Setiausaha Agung PAS dan Setiausaha Agung BERSATU serta bersedia untuk mendedahkannya dalam platform yang lebih sesuai. 

“Satu lagi fakta yang sengaja disembunyikan adalah tindakan BERSATU menghantar nama calon Menteri Besar Perlis adalah tanpa merujuk Majlis Tertinggi PN,” katanya. 

Beliau turut menafikan dakwaan bahawa Presiden PAS, Tan Sri Abdul Hadi Awang sengaja tidak hadir menghadap Tuanku Raja Perlis pada 25 Oktober 2025.

“Tidak pernah Presiden PAS dititah untuk mengadap pada tarikh tersebut, mahupun pada mana-mana tarikh sebelum mahupun selepas kemelut Menteri Besar Perlis berlaku,” tambahnya. 

Kenyataan itu dibuat susulan dakwaan Biro Politik BERSATU yang menzahirkan rasa kesal terhadap kenyataan Abdul Hadi Awang yang membangkitkan beberapa isu berkait hubungan kedua-dua parti dalam PN.
